title: AI for Teachers
description: Where AI saves real hours in a teaching week and where it costs more than it saves. Covers planning, differentiated materials, marking that pupils still trust, and what to tell students about their own use.

modules.title: The Course
modules.description: Four lessons on using AI in teaching without handing over the judgement that makes a lesson work.

lessons.title: Why Generated Lesson Plans Feel Empty

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Ask for a lesson plan on any topic and something arrives immediately: objectives, a starter, a main activity, a plenary. It looks like a plan and teaches like a template.

What is missing is not detail. It is everything you know about the twenty-nine people in the room, and none of that was in the request.

blocks.heading: The Class Is the Missing Input
blocks.bodyHtml:
«Write a lesson plan on photosynthesis for Year 8.»

«Year 8, mixed ability, forty minutes, no lab access this week. Six students read well below level. They did respiration last term and confused the two.»

The second produces something you could actually run on Tuesday, because the constraints that shape a real lesson are finally in the room.

blocks.text: A plan that would work in any classroom will not work well in yours.

blocks.heading: What to Put in Every Request
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Time you really have — after registration and settling
  • What they already met, and what they got wrong last time
  • The spread — the range you are planning for, not the average
  • Your constraints — no printer, no lab, shared equipment

Four lines. They are the difference between a template and a plan.

blocks.question: Your generated plan is fine but generic. Which detail usually fixes it fastest?

options.label: Asking for more activities so there is plenty of material to choose from.
Naming what this class already got wrong the last time you taught it.
Requesting a more engaging and creative style for the whole lesson.
Specifying the exact curriculum reference the lesson is meant to cover.

blocks.successBody: A known misconception gives the plan something specific to work against, which is what makes a lesson feel targeted. Curriculum references and extra activities add volume without adding aim.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which detail only you could supply about this particular class.

blocks.heading: Use It for the Second Version
blocks.bodyHtml:
The strongest use is not writing a plan from nothing. It is adapting one you already trust: same lesson, lower reading level; same lesson, twenty minutes; same lesson, no equipment.

That work is genuinely slow by hand and genuinely fast with a tool, and it keeps your judgement in the plan.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take a lesson you have taught and liked, and paste your own outline.
Ask for a version at a lower reading level, keeping the activities.
Ask for a twenty-minute version for a shortened period.
Note which parts it cut — that tells you what it thought was optional.

blocks.heading: Keep the Bit That Is Yours
blocks.bodyHtml:
Whatever the plan says, the parts that make a lesson land are the example that fits this class, the question you know will start an argument, and the pupil you plan to ask first.

None of that can be generated. It is also, reliably, the part that takes five minutes rather than fifty.

blocks.body: Generated plans feel empty because the class was never described. Give the real time, the prior misconception, the ability spread and your practical constraints — and use the tool mostly to adapt lessons you already trust rather than to invent new ones.

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Preparation, not planning, is where teaching hours actually disappear: the differentiated worksheet, the six extra practice questions, the version for the pupil who was absent.

This is the work AI is genuinely good at, and it is also where the checking has to be fastest.

blocks.heading: Ask for Variants, Not Content
blocks.bodyHtml:
«Make a worksheet about fractions.»

«Here are my six questions. Make three versions: same numbers with more scaffolding, same difficulty with different contexts, and a harder extension using the same method.»

The second keeps your material and your judgement about difficulty, and produces exactly what a mixed class needs.

blocks.text: Your questions, three difficulty levels: that is twenty minutes of work in two.

blocks.heading: Four Materials Worth Generating
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Differentiated versions of a sheet you already use
  • Extra practice in the same format as your examples
  • Plain-language explanations for a pupil who missed the lesson
  • Parent-facing summaries of what is being covered and why

All four are repetitive, low-risk and immediately checkable by reading them once.

blocks.question: You need practice questions for tomorrow. What is the fastest reliable approach?

options.label: Ask for twenty new questions on the topic and pick the usable ones.
Give your six best questions and ask for more in exactly that format.
Ask for a complete worksheet including instructions and answer key.
Describe the topic in detail and let it choose the question types itself.

blocks.successBody: Your own questions carry your judgement about difficulty, phrasing and what the class has met. Matching that format produces questions you can trust after a quick read, rather than twenty you must triage.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which approach keeps the standard you have already set for this class.

blocks.heading: Check the Answers Yourself
blocks.bodyHtml:
Generated answer keys are wrong often enough to matter, and a wrong key in front of a class costs more than the sheet saved.

Work through the questions yourself before printing. For most sheets that is three minutes, and it is not optional.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take a worksheet you use and generate a scaffolded version of it.
Generate an extension set at the same difficulty as your hardest question.
Work through every answer yourself before it reaches a pupil.
Note how long the whole thing took compared with writing it by hand.

blocks.heading: Build a Bank, Not a One-Off
blocks.bodyHtml:
Save the request that produced good material, not just the material. Next year the same prompt with a new topic gives you the same standard in one step.

Over a couple of terms this quietly becomes the most useful file you own, and it belongs to you rather than to any particular tool.

blocks.body: Preparation is where the hours go, so generate variants of material you already trust: differentiated versions, extra practice in your format, catch-up explanations and parent summaries. Always work the answers yourself, and save the prompts rather than only the sheets.

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Marking is the heaviest recurring load in teaching, so it is the first place people want to automate — and the place where automating badly does the most damage.

Feedback works because a pupil believes someone read their work. Anything that breaks that belief costs more than the time it saved.

blocks.heading: Draft the Frame, Write the Substance
blocks.bodyHtml:
Pasting a pupil's essay and sending back whatever comes out.

Marking it yourself in three notes, then asking for those notes to be turned into feedback in your usual tone, at their reading level.

The judgement stays yours; the rewriting into kind, clear sentences is the part that took forty minutes across a class.

blocks.text: Feedback works because a pupil believes someone read it. Protect that belief above all.

blocks.heading: What Must Stay Human
blocks.bodyHtml:
• The judgement — what is good, what is wrong, what grade
  • Anything personal — effort, progress, a hard term at home
  • The next step — you know what this pupil can do next
  • Anything a parent may see — read every word before it leaves

What can be handed over is phrasing, length and consistency across thirty scripts.

blocks.question: You have thirty essays to mark by Friday. What is the sound approach?

options.label: Paste each essay and send the generated comments after a quick read.
Mark each yourself in three notes, then expand those into full comments.
Generate comments for the weakest scripts and write the strongest by hand.
Ask for a grade and comment together, then adjust anything that looks off.

blocks.successBody: Expanding your own notes keeps every judgement yours while removing the slow part — turning shorthand into readable, consistent comments. The other options hand over the assessment itself.
blocks.wrongHint: Ask which part of marking is judgement and which part is typing.

blocks.heading: Watch for Sameness
blocks.bodyHtml:
Thirty comments generated the same way start to read identically, and pupils notice faster than adults expect. They compare.

Vary the opening line yourself, and make sure at least one sentence in each could only have been written about that pupil's work.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Mark five pieces with three shorthand notes each.
Expand one set into full feedback in your own tone.
Read it as the pupil would and check it names something specific.
Compare the time against marking the other four by hand.

blocks.heading: Tell Them What You Do
blocks.bodyHtml:
Being open with pupils and parents about how feedback is produced costs nothing and prevents the conversation you would least like to have.

«I write the judgements; a tool helps me write them up clearly» is honest, easy to say, and most people find it entirely reasonable.

blocks.body: Keep judgement, personal comment and next steps human; hand over phrasing, length and consistency. Mark in shorthand notes and expand them, make sure each comment names something specific to that pupil, and be open about how the write-up is produced.

lessons.title: What to Tell Students About AI

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Students are already using these tools, whatever any policy says. The question is not whether to allow it but what they understand about it.

A ban with no explanation teaches them to hide it. An honest conversation teaches them where it helps and where it quietly costs them something.

blocks.heading: Name What Is Actually Lost
blocks.bodyHtml:
«It's cheating» is a rule. Rules get worked around when nobody explains them.

«Don't use AI for your homework.»

«If it writes your first draft, you skip the part where you find out what you actually think. That struggle is the lesson — the essay is just evidence of it.»

The second is arguable, which is exactly why it works better than an instruction.

blocks.text: A rule without a reason teaches concealment, not judgement.

blocks.heading: Three Rules Students Can Follow
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Say what you used and where — a line at the end, no penalty for honesty
  • You must be able to explain every sentence — if you cannot, it is not yours
  • Never for the thinking step — planning and arguing are the work

These are checkable in conversation, which matters because detection tools are unreliable and accusing a student wrongly does lasting harm.

blocks.question: You suspect a submitted essay was largely generated. What is the sound first step?

options.label: Run it through a detector and act on whatever percentage it returns.
Ask the student to talk you through their argument and their choices.
Give it a zero and explain that generated work receives no marks.
Compare the writing style against their previous submitted work.

blocks.successBody: A conversation is the only reliable test: a student who did the thinking can explain their choices, and one who did not cannot. Detectors produce false positives, and a wrong accusation causes lasting damage.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which method could not wrongly accuse a student who actually did the work.

blocks.heading: Show Them Where It Fails
blocks.bodyHtml:
The most convincing lesson is a demonstration. Ask it something in your subject where it is confidently wrong, and take the class through the error together.

Ten minutes of that does more for their scepticism than a term of warnings, and it teaches a habit they will need long after school.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Find one confident error in your subject and save the exchange.
Write your three classroom rules in language a student would repeat.
Decide what you will do when a student declares they used it — reward the honesty.

blocks.heading: Agree It Across the Department
blocks.bodyHtml:
Different rules in different classrooms produce confusion and resentment, and students will point out the inconsistency before you do.

One shared line, even an imperfect one, is worth more than five carefully considered individual policies.

blocks.body: Explain what is lost rather than issuing a ban: the thinking is the lesson. Use three checkable rules — declare it, be able to explain every sentence, never outsource the thinking — settle suspicion by conversation rather than detectors, and agree the line across the department.
